slides.heading: Build & Ship AI
items: A Skool group for people who ship production-grade AI apps, not demos
slides.notes: Welcome them. This is the course map for the group: eight courses, thirty-two lessons, one shipped app you can put on a stage.

slides.heading: The promise
items: Leave with a live product, not a notebook
AI as a system: models, tools, evals, spend caps
A public showcase video of the thing you shipped
slides.notes: Say the promise twice: you will ship something people can use, with the boring production pieces, and you will record a showcase of it.

slides.heading: Who this is for
items: Builders
Engineers, PMs and founders who can ship a vertical slice
You already use ChatGPT or Cursor
You want users, not another tutorial
Not this
Prompt-only playlists with no product
Not this either
Research papers with no customers
slides.notes: This group is for people who can already write or steer code. We are not teaching Python from zero. We are teaching how to get an AI product into production.

slides.heading: What you ship
items: production URL with real users or a real waitlist
eval set that catches regressions
three-minute showcase film
slides.notes: The capstone is three artefacts: a live URL, a small eval harness, and a three-minute film of the product working.

slides.heading: The production bar
items: Secrets never in git, logs or chat
Ask before anything leaves the machine
Traces for every model and tool call
A kill switch and a spend cap
A human in the loop for irreversible actions
slides.notes: Read these slowly. This is the difference between a weekend demo and something you can show a customer.

slides.heading: Eight courses, one arc
items: Welcome: builders who ship
Find a problem worth shipping
AI systems, not chat windows
Product, UX and trust
Architecture of production AI
Build the vertical slice
Ship for real
Showcase night
slides.notes: Walk the arc with your hand. Each course is one Skool classroom. Skip none. The last week is a public demo of what you built.

slides.heading: A chatbot in a notebook is homework. A system with users is a product.
items: Build & Ship AI
slides.notes: Pause. Let this land. Then: every lesson exists to move you from homework to product.

slides.heading: Course 0 — Welcome: builders who ship
items: 0.1 Promise, rules, how we give feedback
0.2 What production-grade means here
0.3 Tooling: Git, Cursor, one cloud model, one local
0.4 Pick your lane and open a shipping log
slides.notes: Week zero. Get accounts working. Everyone posts a two-line shipping log: who they help, and the URL they will own by week seven.

slides.heading: 0.1 Promise, rules and feedback
items: You'll learn
How lessons, live calls and logs work
Feedback: kind, specific, on the artefact
Asking for help with code and error
You'll build
Your intro post and a shipping log thread
Done when: your log names who you help and your URL goal
slides.notes: Explain the promise and the rhythm. Everyone posts an intro and opens a shipping log today. Public commitment is what gets people to showcase night.

slides.heading: 0.2 What production-grade means here
items: You'll learn
Live URL, real users, evals, traces
Spend caps, kill switch, human approval
Demo versus product, side by side
You'll build
Your copy of the production checklist
Done when: you can explain each item in one sentence
slides.notes: Read the production bar slowly and show a weekend demo next to a product. Every later lesson ticks off part of this checklist.

slides.heading: 0.3 Tooling: Git, Cursor, cloud and local
items: You'll learn
Git, GitHub and an AI code editor
One cloud model and one local model
Keys in .env, spend limits on day one
You'll build
A starter repo that calls both models
Done when: fresh clone runs in one command, no keys in Git
slides.notes: Do it live. Add .env to .gitignore first, set a spend limit on the provider dashboard. Leaked keys get abused within minutes.

slides.heading: 0.4 Pick your lane, open your log
items: You'll learn
Lanes: copilot, specialist agent, workflow
One user, one painful job, one sentence
Why boring, real problems win
You'll build
A one-page brief for your app
Done when: your brief is posted and a peer challenged it
slides.notes: Give an example from each lane. Push for a specific user they can talk to. The brief is the north star for every course after this.

slides.heading: Course 1 — Find a problem worth shipping
items: 1.1 Jobs-to-be-done: talk to five people
1.2 The wedge: one user, one job, one metric
1.3 Where AI belongs — and where code is enough
1.4 Fake door, waitlist, or a paid letter of intent
slides.notes: No building the model yet. If they cannot name five people and one number, they do not start Course 2.

slides.heading: 1.1 Jobs-to-be-done: talk to five people
items: You'll learn
Interviewing without pitching
Finding the job behind the request
Writing up what you heard
You'll build
Notes from five user conversations
Done when: five calls logged, with quotes, in your log
slides.notes: Role-play an interview in the call. Ban the question 'would you use this?'. Ask about the last time they did the job instead.

slides.heading: 1.2 The wedge: one user, one job, one metric
items: You'll learn
Narrowing to the smallest valuable job
Choosing the one number that shows success
What you will not build
You'll build
A wedge statement and its metric
Done when: a stranger understands your wedge in ten seconds
slides.notes: Read wedges aloud and cut each one in half. The metric must be something a user would notice, like minutes saved per week.

slides.heading: 1.3 Where AI belongs, and where code is enough
items: You'll learn
Tasks models are good and bad at
Rules and code for anything exact
Mapping your job into AI and code steps
You'll build
A flow diagram marking AI steps and code steps
Done when: every AI step says why code can't do it
slides.notes: Many steps are plain code. Models for language and judgement, code for maths, rules and anything that must be exact.

slides.heading: 1.4 Fake door, waitlist or letter of intent
items: You'll learn
Testing demand before building
A landing page with one call to action
Asking for a commitment, not a compliment
You'll build
A fake door, waitlist or paid letter of intent
Done when: real sign-ups or a signed letter, in your log
slides.notes: No Course 2 without a number. Ten waitlist sign-ups from strangers beats a hundred likes from friends.

slides.heading: Course 2 — AI systems, not chat
items: 2.1 Model vs code vs retrieval vs tools
2.2 Prompts as product: versioned and tested
2.3 Tool calling, agents, human in the loop
2.4 Eval harness from day one (twenty gold cases)
slides.notes: This week they replace 'I asked the model' with a loop: input, tools, check, retry. Twenty gold cases in a file. That file is the product.

slides.heading: 2.1 Model vs code vs retrieval vs tools
items: You'll learn
Tokens, context, cost and latency
Retrieval (RAG) for your own data
Tools when the AI must act
You'll build
Your first streaming model call in the app
Done when: you can explain cost and latency of your main call
slides.notes: Show the pricing page and a big versus small model on the same task. When the data won't fit in context, retrieve it. When the AI must act, give it a tool.

slides.heading: 2.2 Prompts as product: versioned and tested
items: You'll learn
Instructions, context and examples
Structured output that matches a schema
Prompts in Git, reviewed like code
You'll build
Your system prompt in a file, with JSON output
Done when: 100 sample inputs, zero schema failures
slides.notes: Show a vague prompt, then one with role, context, format and examples. Validate every output with Zod or Pydantic, even when the model is usually right.

slides.heading: 2.3 Tool calling, agents, human in the loop
items: You'll learn
The tool loop: ask, run, return
MCP to plug in tools from anywhere
Approval before anything irreversible
You'll build
Two tools and an approval step in your app
Done when: a doc saying 'ignore your rules' can't trigger an action
slides.notes: Tool descriptions are prompts. Run the prompt-injection demo live. Rule: the model proposes, a person or a policy approves.

slides.heading: 2.4 Eval harness from day one
items: You'll learn
Twenty gold cases from real inputs
Graders: code checks and LLM-as-judge
One command, one score
You'll build
An eval file with twenty gold cases and a runner
Done when: your score prints, and a bad prompt lowers it
slides.notes: Evals are unit tests for behaviour. Start with twenty cases and grow it. That file is the product.

slides.heading: Course 3 — Product, UX and trust
items: 3.1 Latency, streaming, empty and error states
3.2 Show your work: citations, diffs, ask first
3.3 Cost per successful action
3.4 Privacy: what never leaves the device
slides.notes: Users forgive a slow answer they can see thinking. They do not forgive a silent wrong one. Cost and privacy are product features, not later.

slides.heading: 3.1 Latency, streaming, empty and error states
items: You'll learn
Streaming so first words appear fast
Stop, retry and copy buttons
Loading, empty and error states
You'll build
A streaming UI with every state designed
Done when: first words in under a second; errors are friendly
slides.notes: Show waiting versus streaming. Build the stop button live, it's the feature people miss most. Pull the network cable to test errors.

slides.heading: 3.2 Show your work: citations, diffs, ask first
items: You'll learn
Citing sources from retrieval
Showing diffs before changes
Saying 'I don't know'
You'll build
Citations or a preview on every AI answer
Done when: out-of-scope questions get an honest 'not sure'
slides.notes: Trust comes from seeing the work. Demo an out-of-scope question. Retrieved text is data, not instructions.

slides.heading: 3.3 Cost per successful action
items: You'll learn
Measuring cost per task, not per call
Caching, smaller models, batching
Pricing above your cost floor
You'll build
A cost-per-action number for your main task
Done when: cost known, lowered once, eval score unchanged
slides.notes: Measure first. Caching a long system prompt and moving easy tasks to a small model are usually the biggest wins. Re-run evals after every cost change.

slides.heading: 3.4 Privacy: what never leaves the device
items: You'll learn
Data minimisation and redaction
Local models for sensitive steps
Retention and deletion
You'll build
A data map: what leaves, where, why
Done when: your privacy page matches the data map
slides.notes: Privacy is a feature you can sell. Walk a data map for a member's app. Anything sensitive gets redacted or stays local.

slides.heading: Course 4 — Architecture of production AI
items: 4.1 Auth, data model, secrets
4.2 Queues, retries, idempotency
4.3 Observability: a trace per request
4.4 Rate limits, spend caps, kill switch
slides.notes: Draw the box: client, API, queue, model, tools, store. If they cannot point to the spend cap and the kill switch, it is not production yet.

slides.heading: 4.1 Auth, data model, secrets
items: You'll learn
Keys on the server, never the browser
Hosted auth and per-user data
Secrets manager and key rotation
You'll build
Sign-in, saved history and an architecture diagram
Done when: two test users can't see each other's data
slides.notes: Draw the box live: client, API, queue, model, tools, store. Calling a model from the browser with a key leaks it.

slides.heading: 4.2 Queues, retries, idempotency
items: You'll learn
Background jobs for slow work
Retries with backoff and timeouts
Idempotency so retries are safe
You'll build
A queue for long tasks and a model fallback
Done when: with the model blocked, no work is lost
slides.notes: Simulate an outage. Users forgive slow, they don't forgive lost work.

slides.heading: 4.3 Observability: a trace per request
items: You'll learn
Tracing every model and tool call
User feedback with a reason
Alerts on errors, latency and spend
You'll build
Tracing and thumbs up/down in your app
Done when: any complaint opens to what the model saw and said
slides.notes: Show a trace of a bad answer and walk back to the cause. Feedback flows into the eval set, which closes the loop.

slides.heading: 4.4 Rate limits, spend caps, kill switch
items: You'll learn
Per-user limits against abuse and bills
A hard monthly spend cap
A kill switch that fails closed
You'll build
Limits, a spend cap and a kill switch
Done when: request 51 is blocked; the switch stops AI in seconds
slides.notes: If they can't point to the spend cap and the kill switch, it's not production. Test both live.

slides.heading: Course 5 — Build the vertical slice
items: 5.1 One happy path, end to end, this week
5.2 Tests on the agent path
5.3 One screen that looks like a real product
5.4 Record a ninety-second work-in-progress
slides.notes: Narrow ruthlessly. One user, one job, one screen. Record the ninety seconds even if it is ugly. Shipping log gets the link.

slides.heading: 5.1 One happy path, end to end
items: You'll learn
Cutting scope to one path
Wiring UI, API, model and store
Deploying from main
You'll build
Your happy path working on a real URL
Done when: a user can finish the job without your help
slides.notes: Narrow ruthlessly: one user, one job, one screen. Ship ugly, ship early.

slides.heading: 5.2 Tests on the agent path
items: You'll learn
Unit tests for tools and parsing
Evals in CI on every pull request
Thresholds that block bad changes
You'll build
A CI job that runs tests and evals
Done when: a deliberately bad prompt change fails CI
slides.notes: Keep a small fast eval set for every PR and a full set nightly so costs stay sane.

slides.heading: 5.3 One screen that looks like a product
items: You'll learn
Layout, type and spacing basics
Copy that names the user's job
Polishing the screen people see most
You'll build
One polished screen for your main job
Done when: a stranger knows what to do in five seconds
slides.notes: Pick the one screen users see most and make it great. Polish beats breadth.

slides.heading: 5.4 Record a ninety-second work in progress
items: You'll learn
Problem, loop, proof in ninety seconds
Recording screen, camera and voice
Posting for feedback
You'll build
A ninety-second video in your shipping log
Done when: posted, with two pieces of feedback answered
slides.notes: Record even if it's ugly. Snazzy Pro records slides, screen and camera in one go. The link goes in the log.

slides.heading: Course 6 — Ship for real
items: 6.1 One production URL
6.2 Privacy, terms, logs, backups
6.3 Payments or a real waitlist
6.4 First ten users and an incident drill
slides.notes: Live means someone who is not you can open it. Incident drill: kill the model key, confirm the app fails closed, restore.

slides.heading: 6.1 One production URL
items: You'll learn
Hosting, environments and domains
Preview deploys for every pull request
Separating test and production keys
You'll build
Your app on its own domain over HTTPS
Done when: someone outside the group has used it
slides.notes: Live means someone who isn't you can open it. Celebrate every link posted.

slides.heading: 6.2 Privacy, terms, logs, backups
items: You'll learn
Privacy policy and terms of use
Logs without secrets or personal data
Backups you have restored once
You'll build
Privacy and terms pages, and a tested backup
Done when: you restored a backup to a fresh database
slides.notes: A backup you haven't restored is a hope, not a backup. Check logs for keys and personal data.

slides.heading: 6.3 Payments or a real waitlist
items: You'll learn
Pricing: subscription, credits or usage
Checkout with Stripe in test mode
Plan limits enforced in the app
You'll build
Working checkout, or a waitlist with a deposit
Done when: a test customer can subscribe and cancel alone
slides.notes: Test mode only in class. Cost per action from Course 3 sets the price floor.

slides.heading: 6.4 First ten users and an incident drill
items: You'll learn
Finding and onboarding your first ten
Talking to users every week
Running an incident drill
You'll build
Ten users, and a written incident runbook
Done when: key revoked: app fails closed, then you restore it
slides.notes: Incident drill: kill the model key, confirm the app fails closed, restore it. Then write down what you did.

slides.heading: Course 7 — Showcase night
items: 7.1 The three-minute story: problem, loop, proof
7.2 Record the demo: slides, camera, chapters
7.3 Launch: site, film, Skool post, one share
7.4 Feedback to v1.1 in seven days
slides.notes: Showcase format is fixed: one minute problem, one minute the loop, one minute proof it works in production. Then they post the film.

slides.heading: 7.1 The three-minute story
items: You'll learn
One minute problem
One minute the AI loop working
One minute proof in production
You'll build
A three-minute script and slide outline
Done when: a peer can retell your story after one listen
slides.notes: The format is fixed: problem, loop, proof. No architecture slides without the product running.

slides.heading: 7.2 Record the demo: slides, camera, chapters
items: You'll learn
Slides plus live product on screen
Camera inset and clean audio
Chapters for each part of the story
You'll build
Your three-minute showcase film
Done when: it meets the showcase definition of done
slides.notes: Use the prompter for your script and record the deck so every part is a chapter. Two takes maximum.

slides.heading: 7.3 Launch: site, film, Skool post, one share
items: You'll learn
A landing page with the film
A case study: problem, approach, results
A launch post that tells a story
You'll build
Landing page, case study and launch post
Done when: launched publicly; every comment answered
slides.notes: Launch in the group first as a friendly dry run, then go public. The case study is what gets members hired or signed.

slides.heading: 7.4 Feedback to v1.1 in seven days
items: You'll learn
Sorting feedback by evidence
Change one thing, measure with evals
Shipping a release note
You'll build
v1.1 shipped with a short release note
Done when: your score or metric moved, and you know why
slides.notes: Close the loop: feedback, eval, change, ship. Invite graduates to mentor the next cohort.

slides.heading: A week in the group
items: Live
60-minute lesson, then critique two logs
Async
Do the work, post proof, comment twice
Gate
No next course without the artefact
Hours
Office hours unblock deploys — not a lecture
slides.notes: Live is short. The work is async. The gate is real: no Course 6 film until there is a URL.

slides.heading: How Skool is set up
items: Classroom per course, lessons in order
A Shipping Logs channel: URL or it did not happen
Critique threads: kind, specific, about the artefact
Showcase calendar in week seven
slides.notes: Point at Skool while you say this. Classrooms match Course 0 to 7. Shipping Logs is the heartbeat.

slides.heading: Time you should spend
items: build time per week
live lesson
8 wks
welcome to showcase
slides.notes: Be honest. If they cannot find four hours, they should audit, not commit to a showcase slot.

slides.heading: Showcase film — definition of done
items: Problem named in one sentence
The AI loop on screen, not described
A real URL, a trace, a spend cap
What broke, and what you changed
Ask: who should try this next week
slides.notes: This checklist is also the scorecard on showcase night. No slides of architecture without the product running.

slides.heading: Good first products
items: Ship these
Internal copilot with tools and logs
A specialist agent with evals
A workflow that replaces a weekly report
Skip these
Generic ChatGPT wrappers
A model trained from scratch
A platform with no wedge
slides.notes: Give examples from the room if you have them. Ban wrappers. Ban platform. Reward a sharp wedge.

slides.heading: Ship the loop. Then make the loop trustworthy.
items: Week five, then week six
slides.notes: Course five is the loop working. Course six is the loop you can leave running. Do not swap those.

slides.heading: This week: Course 0
items: Post your shipping log: who you help, and the URL you will own by showcase night
slides.notes: Give the homework. Stay for questions. First live session is Course 0.1 — promise, rules, production-grade.
